newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Positive outlook for NZ shares in 1997 - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Positive outlook for NZ shares in 1997 - analysts.

text.p: The New Zealand share market took a solid step forward in 1996 after languishing for nearly a decade in the wake of the '87 equities crash, and it looks set for another step up in 1997, analysts said on Tuesday.
The October general election caused a brief hiccup for domestic investors but ongoing foreign investment interest was sufficient to counter it and the net effect was minimal.

New Zealand Stock Exchange chairman David Wale said he was pleased with the year's results, and the outlook for 1997 was positive as long as the new National-New Zealand First government can restrain its penchant to spend its surpluses.

"We now look forward to a year of consolidation in the market and continued growth, particularly if the coalition government can control its basic urge to spend our money more freely for us," he said.
The indicator NZSE40 capital index rose nine percent to 2,344 during 1996. Market capitalisation reached an all-time high of NZ$55.3 billion.

Ord Minnett Director of Equities John Rattray told Reuters the stockmarket's fundamentals were sound, helped along by a dramatic fall in interest rates over the past six months. Ord Minnett expects rates to fall further and the currency to weaken over 1997, which will help the struggling export sector.

"Our expectation would be that certainly in the second half of next year domestic activity increases quite sharply...Those are conditions under which company profitability across the board should do reasonably well," Rattray said.
However, Bob Matthew, chairman of Brierley Investments Ltd, one of the country's biggest investors, said a falling Kiwi dollar could put negative pressure on the stockmarket.
He told Reuters recently that foreign investors had driven the market in 1996, attracted by high yields combined with an appreciating currency.
"I would lean towards the notion that the market has got some potential pressure on it if we manage our interest rates down and if there is significant fiscal policy change," he said.
Rattray agreed it was possible the direction of international investment in New Zealand could change if the currency's trend was widely perceived to have changed.
Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash said earlier this month the New Zealand dollar was nearing the top of its current cycle.

But stocks which dealt in international commodities, such as Fletcher Forest and Fletcher Paper, helped provide a hedge against downside risk, as a weaker currency was offset by higher earnings, Rattray said.

The one-year deferral of tax cuts planned for 1997 may also subdue profits in 1997. It was one reason for the Reserve Bank to downgrade its economic growth forecasts to 1.3 percent in the March 1997 year. But growth will rebound to 2.6 percent in 1998.

Independent investment analyst Brian Gaynor said that while New Zealand's share market did not surge to the extent of Wall Street in 1996, a correction by the Dow Jones Industrials index could inhibit New Zealand equities.
Wall Sreet could easily be seen as overvalued but that did not necessarily mean it would fall, he said.
"You've got an environment that is very, very favourable to business, and that overvaluation could hold or could actually increase. That is what I think will happen," Gaynor said.
However, he said expert opinion was mixed on Wall Street's longer term outlook, and when that market fell it would drag New Zealand stocks down with it.
"Wall Street at some stage is going to turn and fall and when that happens it will affect us because we've got such a high level of overseas ownership.

"There is a fair chance we will have a downturn by the end of next year. The first six or nine months could be good, but...there's a good chance that by the end of next year something will have happened on Wall St and it will adversely affect our market."

Gaynor said companies with a high level of overseas ownership, such as Carter Holt Harvey, Fletcher Challenge and Telecom, would find it extremely difficult to ignore offshore weakness and that would eventually feed down into smaller locally owned stocks.
